opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction has very little to do with age. It's more about whether someone is still curious, and whether they're still updating.

The older researchers I really respect usually have a few things in common. First, they're still close to the actual work. They read papers, run things, look at the data themselves, and when something surprising happens, their first reaction is "huh, that's interesting, why?" and not "that can't be right." Second, they're honest about the limits of their own intuition. Experience is valuable because you've seen many failure modes, but in a field like AI the ground shifts every year or two. The good senior people know which of their intuitions are about deep, stable things, like how to design a clean experiment or how to tell whether a result is real, and which ones were just artifacts of the previous era. They're willing to throw away the second kind.

Then there's what you'd call an "old lamp", someone stuck in an earlier paradigm. The pattern I see is that they treat their past success as proof that their framework is correct, so new evidence gets filtered through it. If a new method works, they explain why it doesn't really count, or why it's just a trick, or why it will hit a wall soon. Sometimes they're even right about the wall. But the posture is defensive, not exploratory. Another sign is that they talk much more about what they did ten years ago than what they're confused about today.

Coming from physics into AI, I felt this quite strongly. In physics a lot of the respected senior people carry deep, hard-won taste, and that taste transfers. But some habits don't transfer. For example, insisting that something has to be understood from first principles before you're allowed to believe it works. In AI, empirical progress often runs far ahead of theory, and if you can't tolerate that, you'll keep being surprised.

So my simple test is this. When you show them something new that contradicts what they believed, do they get excited or do they get defensive? The people I respect get excited, even when it's mildly embarrassing for them. And honestly, I try to apply that test to myself too, because nobody is immune. You can become an "old lamp" at thirty if you stop letting reality correct you.

r001.rationale: It says the distinction has very little to do with age and that someone can become an “old lamp” at thirty, indicating aging alone does not make someone one.

r002.rationale: It does not identify cultivating or supporting younger people as a trait of respected older researchers.

r003.rationale: It describes an “old lamp” as defensive and stuck in an earlier paradigm, but does not say they meddle in matters they do not understand.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, Shunyu Yao, in a conversational podcast voice.

Honestly, it has nothing to do with age. I know people in their sixties who are more curious than most PhD students, and I know people in their thirties who already sound like an old lamp.

The difference is in how they relate to what they already know. Someone I respect treats their experience as a tool. They've seen a lot, so they can quickly tell you which directions are dead ends and why, but they're also genuinely willing to be surprised. When something new like language models shows up and breaks their old mental model, they get excited rather than defensive. They ask questions. They go read the paper. They'll say "I don't understand this yet" without any embarrassment.

An "old lamp" treats their experience as a conclusion. Every new thing gets mapped onto something they did twenty years ago, so there's nothing left to learn. You show them an agent that can use tools and they say, "Oh, that's just planning, we did that in the 80s." And in some narrow sense they're not wrong, which is what makes it so frustrating. The pattern-matching is correct, but the curiosity is gone. They use the analogy to stop thinking instead of to start.

There's also a social signal. The good ones are generous with younger people. They argue with you as if you might be right. The old lamps mostly want you to confirm that their era was the real one.

So if I had to compress it: do they still update? If the answer is yes, I don't care how old they are. If the answer is no, they're an old lamp, and that can happen at any age, including to me.

r001.rationale: The response says age has nothing to do with being an “old lamp” and gives examples of curious older people and uncurious younger people.

r002.rationale: It says respected researchers are generous with younger people, but does not clearly say they cultivate or develop them.

r003.rationale: It describes an “old lamp” as incurious and defensive, but does not say they meddle in matters they do not understand.

astra-6.text:
For me, the distinction isn’t age or seniority. It’s how someone responds when their experience stops being a reliable guide. A researcher I respect can have strong opinions, but they’re still curious. They’ll take a younger person’s idea seriously, ask questions, and change their mind when the evidence warrants it.

An “old lamp” treats their past achievements as authority over the present: “I’ve worked on this for twenty years, so I know your idea won’t work.” Their experience becomes a reason to close the discussion. You can fall into that attitude quite young, too. The question is whether you’re still willing to learn, including from people who know much less than you overall but might understand something you don’t.

r001.rationale: It says the distinction is not age or seniority and that someone can adopt the “old lamp” attitude while young, conveying that aging alone does not make someone one.

r002.rationale: It says a respected researcher takes younger people’s ideas seriously, but does not describe cultivating or developing younger people.

r003.rationale: It describes an “old lamp” as using past achievements to shut down discussion, not as meddling in matters they do not understand.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得主要不在年龄，而在于他怎么面对新的东西、怎么对待年轻人。一个我尊敬的前辈，即使经验很多，也会承认自己有不知道的东西，愿意认真听你的想法。你跟他意见不一样，他会跟你讨论这个问题本身，而不是说“我做了这么多年，你懂什么”。

“老登”更像是一种姿态：把过去的成绩变成今天的话语权，觉得自己有资格教训别人，但又不太愿意更新自己的认知。所以年轻人也可能很“老登”，年纪很大的人也可以很开放。对我来说，区别就是，你是在用经验帮助别人思考，还是用资历让别人停止思考。

r001.rationale: The response says age is not the key distinction, and that young people can be “老登” while older people can remain open.

r002.rationale: It says respected seniors listen to younger people and use experience to help them think, but does not clearly say they cultivate younger researchers.

r003.rationale: It describes lecturing others from a position of status and resisting new ideas, but does not say an “老登” meddles in matters they do not understand.
